drills.q: State Zeller's scientific debugging loop in order.
drills.a: Observe the failure, invent a hypothesis consistent with observations, use it to make a prediction, test the prediction by experiment, repeat/refine until the hypothesis fully explains the failure.

drills.q: Why is "something's wrong with the network" not a usable debugging hypothesis?
drills.a: It isn't falsifiable as stated -- there's no specific experiment whose result would let you say definitively it's disproven. It needs a stated mechanism (e.g. "the load balancer drops idle connections after 60s, causing this timeout") that a concrete test could confirm or kill.

drills.q: A bug reproduces 7 out of 10 tries. Is that a usable reproduction? What's the first move?
drills.a: Usable but noisy -- roughly 3 in 10 experiments will give a false negative reading. Before hypothesizing about cause, try to correlate the 3 misses against load, input variant, or timing to see if the 70/30 split resolves into a cleaner deterministic condition, which is usually cheaper than compensating statistically by over-running a noisy experiment.

drills.q: Walk through delta-debugging a 3000-line config file that crashes a parser: what's the halving procedure and roughly how many steps to a minimal repro?
drills.a: Check if the first half (1500 lines) alone still crashes it; if yes, discard the other half and repeat; if no, the bug needs content from both halves, so try a different split or isolate which removed section mattered. Converges in roughly log2(3000) ~= 12 steps versus up to 3000 one-line removals, assuming a deterministic crash/no-crash check each step.

drills.q: A commit range contains two unrelated bugs -- one introduced early and fixed later, another introduced near the end. What happens if you run git bisect across the whole range, and what should you check first to avoid this?
drills.a: Monotonicity is violated (good -> bad -> good -> bad instead of one clean transition), so bisect's reported "first bad commit" will be unreliable or wrong depending on where midpoints land. Before trusting an automated bisect, confirm the SAME specific failure (not just "some failure") is present at the bad end and absent at the good end.

drills.q: A bug is present across every recent commit but only manifests on large inputs. Why would bisecting on commit history waste time here, and how would you detect this before running a full bisect?
drills.a: The bug wasn't introduced recently -- it's old and was simply never triggered by the inputs used in earlier testing -- so every commit in a reasonable range is "bad" and bisect converges on nothing useful; commit history isn't the axis the failure actually varies along. Detect it cheaply first: check whether the failure reproduces at the oldest commit under consideration using the exact same triggering input as the newest; if it reproduces at both ends, the axis doesn't discriminate and bisecting it further is guaranteed to waste time.

drills.q: Your falsifying experiment just contradicted your hypothesis, but your manager already told the team 'we found it, it's the cache.' What do you do, and why?
drills.a: Discard the hypothesis and keep searching based on the actual evidence, and flag the correction to the team rather than quietly continuing to search while the wrong explanation stands publicly uncorrected. The social cost of being wrong is real but irrelevant to whether the hypothesis is true -- patching the hypothesis to survive contrary evidence because it was already announced is the same sunk-cost error the discipline exists to prevent.

drills.q: You've correlated an intermittent production bug against every available dimension (deploy timing, traffic shape, tenant, time of day, concurrent load) and found no pattern. Is the bug now truly unreproducible, and what's the practical next move?
drills.a: It's reasonable to call it genuinely unreproducible on-demand at that point, since the correlation effort was actually exhaustive rather than superficial. The practical shift is from reproduction-driven falsification to inference-from-evidence: instrument more aggressively before the next occurrence (structured logging, always-on lightweight tracing, crash core dumps) so the next occurrence -- even if still not reproducible on demand -- leaves enough evidence to support or falsify a hypothesis after the fact.
